title: How the day closed
text: It was a rough Monday for tech. The Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ fell 2.7% and the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 1.9%. Chip stocks fell the most: on our list, the five AI supplier stocks dropped about 5.3% on average, while the four big AI platform companies dropped about 2.7%. Many traders sold before NVIDIA's results on Tuesday after the close. Safer, slower movers held up better: the dividend fund SCHD slipped only 0.7% and Eli Lilly 0.6%.

title: NVIDIA is near its one year low before its report
text: NVIDIA fell 4.1% to $156.14. That is only about 5% above its lowest price of the past year ($148.80) and 7.8% of the way up its one year range. It reports results on Tuesday, November 17, after the market closes. The average analyst target is $311.16, but a target is only a guess. After a report, a stock can jump or drop a lot in one day, in either direction.

title: Chip suppliers fell harder than the big platforms
text: Vertiv fell 6.6%, TSMC 6.3%, AMD 5.6% and Broadcom 3.9%. Microsoft fell only 1.1%. Companies that sell parts for AI, like chips and cooling gear, tend to swing more than the giant companies that buy them. Rocket Lab, which is not an AI stock, also fell 6.8%, showing that nervous days hit jumpy stocks hardest.

title: Alphabet slips close to its one year low
text: Alphabet fell 4.1% to $283.72, about 4% above its one year low of $272.11. It is one of the cheapest big AI names on our list by price to earnings, at about 14.5. Alphabet and Amazon own pieces of Anthropic, an AI company planning to sell stock to the public this week, so news about that sale may move them.

title: Fed notes on Wednesday
text: On Wednesday at 2 pm New York time, the Federal Reserve releases the notes from its October meeting. Traders think the Fed may raise rates in December. The 10 year Treasury yield averaged 5.13% in October, the highest month on our chart. Higher rates can make fast growing stocks less attractive.

title: Lesson 53: What is index weighting?
text: An index like the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq 100 is a list of companies whose prices are blended into one number. But not every company counts the same. Most big indexes give more weight to bigger companies, measured by market value (share price times number of shares). Think of a class average where the tallest kids count three times: if they have a bad day, the whole average drops. That is why a fall in a few giants like NVIDIA, Microsoft and Alphabet can pull a whole fund like QQQ down, even if many smaller companies in it did fine. When you own an index fund, check which companies make up the biggest slices.
